rv.q: “Ohio State Murders” leaves a lasting imprint—I picture a bloody handprint—on what for lack of a better term I’ll call the soul.
Ohio State Murders represents an extraordinary Broadway debut for Kennedy and a triumphant return for McDonald.
When an exception takes root, with a team of artists as visionary as these, it's certainly worth the wait.
McDonald's performance is a master class in controlled emotion, as she navigates the treacherous terrain of memory and trauma with grace and power.
What Kenny Leon's production delivers most potently is Morrison in full command of her towering gifts, spinning out her story with the mesmerizing authority of a master storyteller.

In its bracing Broadway debut—which also marks the Broadway debut of Kennedy, now 91—both the old and young versions are played by Audra McDonald, who toggles between the two with the masterful emotional control and variety we have come to expect from her.
You believe her as this idealistic college woman, progressively shattered by what she finds as an unwelcome Buckeye.

And even though Kenny Leon’s plain direction threatens to flatten the rocky beauty of “Ohio,” this production ultimately reaffirms Kennedy’s singular mastery of common language, dissolution of traditional form and rightful place on Broadway.
In “Ohio State Murders,” Kennedy, an avant-gardist who deserves a place among our most honored and produced playwrights, does it in many, each of them a bullet.
It's an absorbing, observant and admirably peculiar character study with stinging parallels to today.
It’s in the portrayal of those contrasts that McDonald finds something close to perfection in a flawed production.
You are left with the feeling of wishing for something stranger, and also of seeing those accommodations more clearly.
But Ohio State Murders stumbles given its concealed retelling.
The audience gasps and tears that accompany the performance are honestly earned and, I expect, unforgettable.
Ohio State Murders bests them all.
This is a story executed in exquisite detail and delicacy that pierces you like a scalpel.
McDonald’s truly mesmerizing performance holds so much emotion, so many cadences, and is also a barely suppressed scream.
Cheers to Audra McDonald and company to bringing it so rivetingly to life.
McDonald elevates this to an acting tour de force as she plays the same woman 40 years apart as well as shifting mood over and over again.
By the play’s end, that overly studied reserve may be the only thing that keeps this character from absolutely exploding with rage.
By the end, you'll understand the natural response: Try opening a history book, or looking around you.
It’s a shocking, disturbing and unsettling experience.
The experience is brief, powerful, and entirely worth it.
This is a murder mystery of sorts, after all, so put on your detective's hat and keep your eyes and ears peeled for the clues.
Her decades-old testimony has lost none of its sting.

McDonald does a remarkable job relating to the “babies”, and we see Suzanne’s rapid growing-up process through the shift in the ways she handles them: dull fear and resignation when they’re first placed in her arms, an anxious tenderness when she has to take one to the doctor.
The repetition is unnecessary, especially in a piece that, sadly, doesn’t always hold one’s attention.
There is some irony, then, that I actually liked this version of “Ohio State Murders” somewhat less than a production of the same eerie, riveting, challenging play that I saw early last year.
Kenny Leon's production is handsome and respectful, but it feels more like a reverent museum piece than a living, breathing work of theater.
One could just as easily ask, why is it on Broadway at all.
In the meantime, McDonald gives yet another performance of a lifetime, and chances are a seventh Tony Award isn’t far behind.
She’s riveting, devastating, and mesmerizing.
Will Audra McDonald win another Tony for this tour de force performance?
What could have been an interesting tale of overcoming horror yet succumbing to horror, is limited in range and dreadfully dreary.
But it’s essentially unsatisfying.
To add further significance, it stars top caliber actress Audra McDonald, who gives one of the year’s finest performances.

cn.t: Critics praise Audra McDonald's searing performance in Adrienne Kennedy's long-overdue Broadway debut, though some find the 75-minute monologue-heavy work more reverent than dramatically vital. The production earns respect as a significant cultural moment.
